metric_rationale: The design contains 10 of 16 trial types where TTB and Tallying make different modal predictions: conflict trials (1-6, 13-14; 48 of 96 trials) where the top cue favors one option but the cue majority favors the other, and tally-tie trials (7-8; 12 of 96 trials) where the tally is 2-2 so Tallying must guess at exactly 50% while TTB is confident via the top cue. The metric recomputes both heuristics row-by-row from the ratings and the known validities, keeps only these dissociation rows, and returns P(choose the TTB-predicted option) - 0.5. Under TTB, every dissociation trial is chosen with probability (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 > 0.5, so the metric is positive (approaching +0.5 for large beta). Under Tallying, the 48 conflict trials are chosen at (1-eps)*sigmoid(-beta*margin) + eps/2 < 0.5 and the 12 tie trials at exactly 0.5, so the metric is negative (approaching -0.4 for large beta). The sign itself flips between theories, giving a large mean gap (e.g., ~0.66 at beta=2, eps=0.1; still ~0.065 even at the near-degenerate beta=0.1, eps=0). Per-subject variability is pure binomial noise over ~60 trials (sd <= ~0.065 at worst), so Welch's t-test at N=25 yields enormous t-statistics across essentially the whole non-degenerate parameter space. The metric is computed identically on pooled and single-subject data (each subject has all 16 trial types x 6 reps), so between-subject variance is well defined. It avoids hashing any sequence-valued column (no groupby/unique on ratings), and it is not trivially true for TTB: it requires subjects to actually follow the one-reason cascade against the cue majority on the majority of dissociation trials.

The design's core dissociation is the set of CONFLICT trials where the tally majority and the top discriminating cue point to opposite options: the five margin+2 grid cells (trials 1, 4, 7, 10, 13) and the two extreme-conflict trials (20, 21) where one option wins 7 of 8 cues against cue 1. On exactly these trials the two theories make opposite directional predictions: Tallying chooses the majority-winner with probability sigmoid(2*beta) (grid) to sigmoid(6*beta) (extreme), while TTB chooses the cue-winner with probability sigmoid(beta), i.e. the tally-winner only 1-sigmoid(beta) of the time. The metric is simply the empirical proportion of tally-winner choices on those 7 unique trials x 4 repetitions = 28 conflict observations per subject. This maximizes the mean gap (near 1 vs near 0 for any moderate beta, and still a sizeable gap even at small beta or with lapses, since the extreme-conflict trials alone span sigmoid(6*beta) vs 1-sigmoid(beta)) while keeping between-subject variance at binomial level over 28 trials (~p(1-p)/28), so 25 human subjects easily separate the theories via Welch's t-test. Trials where the heuristics agree (M=-2 cells, anchors) and tie trials are deliberately excluded: they carry no discriminative signal and would only dilute the contrast and add variance. The metric is a simple proportion, so it is well-defined and stable both on the pooled data and on each single subject's slice.

The metric is a zero-sum linear contrast (weights 2, -1, -1) over choice proportions favoring the TTB winner in three structurally identified trial classes, so it is exactly 0 in expectation for TTB at ANY parameter setting (beta in [0.1,20], epsilon in [0,0.5]): TTB's two structural invariants — one-reason stopping and constant confidence sigmoid(beta) on every discriminating trial — force p_HIGH = p_DEPTH5 = p_REV = p*. For PWEI the three classes sit at very different points of its evidence-margin psychometric: HIGH trials (all cues unanimous, or top cue alone deciding) have |D| ~ 0.4-1 normalized, giving p ~ 0.89-0.92 after lapse; DEPTH5 trials have D ~ 6e-5 (0.70^gamma is ~1e-5 of total weight at gamma in [35,50]), giving p ~ 0.50; REV trials have D negative (0.89^g+0.88^g+0.87^g > 0.90^g throughout the box), giving p ~ 0.12-0.37 — PWEI votes AGAINST the top cue. Hence PWEI's metric value is ~0.9-1.2 across its entire parameter box, vs ~0 for TTB: a sign- and magnitude-robust gap. Per-subject noise is binomial only (24, 12, 12 observations per class): worst-case per-subject SD is ~0.29 (TTB with p*=0.5) and ~0.21 (PWEI), so at N=25 the Welch t-statistic is ~13-16, far below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on a single subject's 96-trial slice, so between-subject variance is well defined. It is falsifiable (human data showing graded confidence or top-cue reversals would push it away from 0), not trivially true: it directly tests TTB's constant-confidence/depth-invariance prediction against actual choices.

Core idea: TTB's structural invariant is that its choice probability is a single constant p* = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 on EVERY trial where any cue discriminates, regardless of cue depth, validity, or lower-cue configuration. PWEI instead produces a graded psychometric function of the power-weighted evidence margin. The metric therefore regresses, trial by trial, the binary indicator 'did the subject choose the TTB winner (the option favored by the first discriminating cue)?' on the PWEI weighted margin D re-signed toward that winner (x = +D if TTB winner is A, -D if B; weights v_j^40 normalized, gamma=40 the midpoint of PWEI's box). Under TTB, E[y|x] = p* for all x, so the OLS slope is exactly 0 for every parameter setting (beta in [0.1,20], eps in [0,0.5]) — this cancels TTB's parameter heterogeneity entirely, leaving only binomial noise. Under PWEI, E[y|x] = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta*x)+eps/2, a strictly increasing psychometric curve; across this design's 11 discriminating cell types the margins span x in [-0.08, 1.0] with predicted conformities from 0.374 (L4: cue-2 winner opposed by all four lower cues) up to 0.90 (all-agree), giving a slope of roughly 0.50-0.59 robustly across PWEI's whole parameter box (checked at gamma=35/beta=7/eps=0.23 -> ~0.52; gamma=50/beta=10/eps=0.17-0.23 -> ~0.50). Per-subject noise: 88 discriminating trials per subject, residual variance ~0.2, Var(x) ~0.10, so per-subject slope sd ~0.15 for both theories (TTB's is at most ~0.17 even at p*=0.5). At N=25 the Welch t on the pooled point estimates is approx 0.55 / sqrt((0.022+0.028)/25) ~ 12, far below alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on each single-subject slice (each subject sees all 24 pairs x 4 reps), so between-subject variance is well defined. Identical-option catch trials (trials 23/24) are excluded because both models guess there and including them would hand TTB a spurious non-zero slope. Mirror trials are handled automatically since x and y are computed from the actual A/B vectors, so side bias cancels in the regression.

The metric is the OLS slope of P(choose the TTB winner) regressed on the inverted-polarity integrated evidence E_w favoring that winner, computed across the 11 evidence cells of this design (each cell = a unique pair + its mirror, 8 trials per subject per cell; 88 discriminating trials per subject, the 2 identical pairs excluded). STRUCTURAL CONTRAST: Under TTB, the probability of choosing the first-discriminating-cue winner is one constant p* = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2 on EVERY discriminating trial, independent of everything happening on lower-validity cues. Hence the cell psychometric function over E_w is exactly flat and the slope is 0 in expectation for any (beta, epsilon) in the parameter box — the per-subject slope carries only binomial noise (sd approx. 0.12 in normalized evidence units, since the wide E_w spread from -1 to +0.58 makes the slope estimator very efficient: Var(slope) approx p*(1-p*) / (8 * Var_cells(E_w))). Under SPI, P(choose winner) = (1-eps)*[(1-rho)*sigma(2*beta*E_w) + rho*sigma(-2*beta*E_w)] + eps/2, which is strictly INCREASING in E_w for any rho < 0.5, any lapse, any beta > 0, and any gamma in [0,2] (the sign/ordering of E_w across cells is robust across gamma because the validities are well separated and the design was built so the deciding cue always dominates). The cells sweep E_w from -1 (unanimously endorsed option, trials 8/20) through -0.57 (trials 1/13) up to +0.58 (trials 7/19), so SPI produces a steep positive slope (approx. 0.55 at the design's example parameters gamma=1, beta=6, eps=0.2, rho=0.1; still approx. 0.15 at weak settings beta=2, rho=0.3, eps=0.3). This is the design's core 'flat vs. monotone ladder' dissociation (dissociations 1-3): TTB is structurally pinned at slope 0 while SPI is structurally pinned away from 0 in the positive direction. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on each subject's slice (every subject completes all 96 trials, so each subject yields all 11 cells), giving a well-defined between-subject variance that is tiny under TTB (pure binomial) and moderate under SPI, so Welch's t-test at N=25 separates the two theories by many standard errors. No trivially-circular quantity is used: the metric only reads choices and the stimulus vectors, and the contrast is TTB's falsifiable one-reason (lower-cue non-use) prediction against SPI's all-cue integration prediction.

METRIC: Among trials where the two options differ in total endorsement count by at least 5 (|n_A - n_B| >= 5), compute p(choose the TTB winner | TTB winner is the DENSER option) minus p(choose the TTB winner | TTB winner is the SPARSER option). These extreme cells are trials 1, 9, 10, 11, 12, 17, 20, 21, 22, 6 (24 conflict trials + 16 agreement trials per subject).

WHY TTB GIVES EXACTLY 0: On every trial where any cue discriminates, TTB's probability of choosing its winner is the same constant p* = (1-eps)*sigmoid(beta) + eps/2, completely independent of the endorsement counts. Both groups (TTB-winner-denser and TTB-winner-sparser) consist only of discriminating trials, so the two conditional proportions have identical expectation p* and the difference is exactly 0 at ANY (beta, epsilon). This is a structural null — no parameter setting can move TTB off zero.

WHY SPI GIVES A LARGE NEGATIVE VALUE: SPI's evidence for the TTB winner on these cells is sign-robust across its entire parameter box (gamma in [0,2], any beta, rho, eps). On conflict trials (TTB winner is denser: trials 1, 9, 11, 12, 20, 22) SPI's weighted evidence for the TTB winner is between -0.6 and -1 (e.g., trial 11: E = -1; trial 1: E in [-0.875, -0.789]), so p(choose TTB winner) < 0.5. On agreement trials (TTB winner is sparser: trials 6, 10, 17, 21) SPI's evidence is between +0.33 and +0.75, so p(choose TTB winner) > 0.5. Hence the difference is negative, and strongly so for any beta > 0 and rho < 0.5 (at gamma=1, beta=6, eps=0.2, rho=0.1 the metric is about -0.43; even at modest beta=2 it is about -0.15).

WHY THE |count difference| >= 5 THRESHOLD: The 1s-count difference is a gamma-robust proxy for SPI's evidence magnitude. Restricting to extreme cells concentrates the signal where SPI's sigmoid is far from 50% on both groups, which maximizes the mean gap per unit of binomial noise; including weak-evidence cells (count diff 1-2) adds mostly noise since SPI is near 50% there. Per subject the metric uses 40 trials, keeping the between-subject standard deviation around 0.10-0.16 (binomial), while the between-theory mean gap is 0.3-0.5 for typical SPI parameters — comfortably detectable with Welch's t-test at N=25, alpha=0.01. The metric works identically on the pooled DataFrame and on single-subject slices (every subject sees all 24 unique pairs x4).

The metric is the mean over subjects of each subject's absolute choice extremity |2p-1| on the 36 near-unanimous trials (one option all-zeros vs. >=7 endorsements; trials T1-T3 and their mirrors T9-T11, 6 reps each). It is computed per subject (so it works on a single subject's slice) and averaged over subjects when given the pooled data, making the pooled point estimate exactly the population mean of the per-subject values. WHY IT SEPARATES THE THEORIES: (1) RFI-delta's architecture is a stable per-subject trait with only a small slip (delta in [0.08,0.12]) and small lapse (eps in [0,0.08]). Every RFI subject -- whether in the anti-endorsement majority (p(sparse) in [0.80,0.92]) or the conventional minority (p(sparse) in [0.08,0.20]) -- is highly consistent on these high-evidence trials, so |2p-1| lands in roughly [0.6, 0.85] for ALL subjects. Expected value ~0.74 with small between-subject variance (~0.02, dominated by binomial noise over 36 trials). The absolute value is crucial: it renders the statistic polarity-symmetric, so RFI's bimodal population does NOT inflate the between-subject variance (both clusters share the same extremity). (2) SPI has no per-subject trait; its heterogeneity comes from wide per-subject boxes eps in [0.05,0.35], rho in [0,0.35], beta in [0.5,20]. The average SPI subject is heavily attenuated toward chance: at sigma~1 the extremity is approximately 1 - eps - 2rho + 2*eps*rho, whose box average is only ~0.5, and the ~13% of subjects with small beta are pulled much closer to 0.5. Expected value ~0.45-0.50 with large between-subject variance (~0.06-0.10) from the wide parameter box. The mean gap (~0.25) combined with RFI's tight per-subject stability yields a Welch t of roughly 4-6 at N=25, well below alpha=0.01, whereas the raw p(sparse) statistic fails because RFI's minority cluster inflates its between-subject variance and pooling dilutes the contrast. The metric is not trivially satisfied by construction: it would falsify RFI if humans showed heterogeneous attenuation (a homogeneous middle), and it would falsify SPI if a large share of subjects were near-chance on unanimous trials.

Both theories share the same per-trial functional form; they differ in how far each subject is pulled away from a deterministic sparse (or dense) preference. RFI-delta mandates a steep beta (>=3), a small slip (delta in [0.08,0.12]) and a tiny lapse (eps <= 0.08), so EVERY RFI subject sits near saturation on high-|E| trials: per-subject p(sparse) in [0.75, 0.92] for the ~95% red-flag majority AND p in [0.08, 0.25] for the ~5% conventional minority. SPI allows a large lapse (eps up to 0.35, mean ~0.20) and a large polarity mixture (rho up to 0.35, mean ~0.175), placing typical SPI subjects at p(sparse) ~ 0.55-0.80 on the same trials. Taking |p_hat - 0.5| (i) makes the metric polarity-AGNOSTIC, so RFI's minority cluster (extremity ~0.32) lands at the same value as its majority (~0.36) instead of injecting huge between-subject mixture variance, and (ii) yields a clean mean contrast: RFI ~0.35 vs SPI ~0.22. The trial filter (endorsement-count difference >= 3, i.e., design cells R3-R8 plus mirrors, 48 trials/subject) is chosen so that the count-sparser option is the inverted-evidence option for every gamma in [0,2] (the E-ladder ordering is gamma-robust by design) and so that per-subject extremity is estimated from 48 Bernoulli trials, giving binomial SD ~0.05-0.07 — small relative to the ~0.13 mean gap. Expected Welch t at N=25 is ~4-5 (p < 0.0005) under uniform parameter sampling from each theory's box, and even larger if parameters are fixed at central values. The function returns the mean of per-subject values on the pooled DataFrame (so the pooled point estimate equals the population mean of the per-subject metric) and the single-subject extremity on a subject slice, satisfying the per-subject variance requirement. Tie trials and low-contrast/conflict trials are excluded, so the metric isolates exactly the attenuation parameter regime where the two theories' boxes are disjoint.
